d.title: The residual is what makes a block a modification rather than a replacement
d.caption: **Two sublayers and two norms: attention mixes information across positions, the FFN transforms each position on its own** — and both are wrapped in a residual connection. That wrapper is the structural claim: **a block computes an *adjustment* to its input, not a new representation**, so a stack of twelve blocks is twelve successive edits to one vector rather than twelve translations. Which is exactly what §05 measures, and why removing a middle block from a trained model degrades it gently rather than breaking it.

nodes.label: So a block is a modification
And a stack is successive edits

d.title: The decoder output has seven positions, not twelve
d.caption: **The sequence length follows the *target*; the source only ever enters through cross-attention's keys and values** — which is what lets a transformer translate a 12-word sentence into a 7-word one, and is the structural difference from an encoder, where output length always equals input length. Note also that the encoder is shape-preserving: **(2, 12, 512) in and out**, which is why encoder blocks stack without any adapter between them.

state: enters as cross-attn K and V

d.title: A decoder block is 1.33x an encoder block, and the extra is one whole module
d.caption: **3,152,384 against 4,204,032, and the difference is exactly 1,050,624 — one complete cross-attention module**, the same size as self-attention. Which is the honest way to think about encoder-decoder cost: **a decoder layer is not slightly more expensive, it has three sublayers instead of two.** And the LayerNorms are 2,048 parameters, **0.06% of the block** — worth remembering next time a normalisation choice is presented as a parameter-budget question.

d.title: The residual stream grows 29% through twelve untrained blocks
d.caption: **Every sublayer reads from the residual stream and adds to it; nothing replaces it, and in a Pre-LN model nothing rescales it either — so its magnitude accumulates.** Measured on an untrained 12-block stack: **RMS 0.9975 at the input, 1.2899 at block 11 — a 1.29× growth with no training at all.** Which is why deep Pre-LN models need care at the output: **the later blocks are writing into a stream that is already louder than what they were initialised against.**

d.title: One mask zeroes a triangle; the other normalises over a different axis entirely
d.caption: The two masks in a decoder are not variations of one idea. **Self-attention is (1, 8, 7, 7) with an upper-triangle max of exactly 0.00e+00 — the causal constraint, enforced to the float.** Cross-attention is **(1, 8, 7, 12), and its rows sum to 1 over the twelve *source* positions** — so there is no triangle to mask, because a target position may legitimately read any part of the source. **Confusing the two is how a causal mask ends up applied to cross-attention and silently halves the available source.**

d.title: Three levels, and only the middle one has no fatal problem
d.caption: The last column is the argument. **Word level: any unseen word becomes UNK and morphology is invisible, at a 500,000+ vocabulary. Character level: a ~128 vocabulary and quadratic attention over very long sequences, with little meaning per token.** Subword keeps common words whole and splits rare ones into pieces it has seen — **`the` is one token, `unhappiness` becomes `un` + `happiness`** — so **frequent words stay short and nothing is ever unrepresentable.**

steps.note: which is why everything uses it

d.title: Two pairs tie for the maximum at nine
d.caption: The initial counts on the four-word corpus put **`(e,r)` and `(r,</w>)` both at 9** — a genuine tie at the top, which is where §03's divergence comes from: **the algorithm as stated does not say which to merge, so the implementation's tie-break decides the vocabulary.** Below them, `(w,e)` at 8 and `(l,o)`/`(o,w)` at 7. The `</w>` end marker is doing real work here: **it makes `er` at the end of a word a different symbol from `er` inside one.**

state: never merged, as it turns out

d.title: Strict greedy and the reference take different merges from merge 3 onward
d.caption: Both agree on merges 1 and 2. **Then strict greedy takes `(l,o)` at frequency 7, because 7 > 6; the reference takes `(n,e)` at 6.** Neither is wrong about the counts — **the reference is following a different ordering convention, and the result is a different vocabulary from identical data.** Which is the practical warning: **a BPE vocabulary is not determined by the corpus alone, so two implementations can both be “correct” and produce different tokenizations.**

d.title: Encoding is the merge list replayed in order, and the fallback is characters
d.caption: **The merges are applied in the order they were learned, which is why encoding is deterministic and why the list is part of the tokenizer rather than just the vocabulary.** `lower` was never seen whole and encodes to **2 tokens** from pieces that were. Then the degradation is visible: **`lowest` is 5 tokens because `e`, `s` and `t` were never merged, and `widest` is 7 — a full character fallback.** So a word's token count depends on how much of it the merge list happened to cover.

d.title: Four names, and one of them is not an algorithm
d.caption: **SentencePiece is a framework rather than an algorithm: it treats the input as a raw byte stream with no pre-tokenisation, so it works on languages without spaces, and it implements both BPE and Unigram.** Which is why “SentencePiece vs BPE” is a category error. And Unigram runs in the opposite direction from the other two: **start with a large vocabulary and *prune* the tokens that least affect corpus likelihood — top-down, where BPE and WordPiece build bottom-up from characters.**

state: a framework: raw bytes, no pre-tok

d.title: Five, seven or eight tokens for the same five words
d.caption: **GPT-2 gives 5 ids, RoBERTa 7 and BERT 8** — and the differences are not all about subwords: RoBERTa adds `<s>` and `</s>`, BERT adds `[CLS]` and `[SEP]`, **and GPT-2 adds nothing.** The genuine split is `transformer`: **BERT breaks it into `transform` + `##er` while GPT-2 and RoBERTa keep it whole.** And the id sequence does not match what is usually quoted — **`[101, 1045, 2293, 10938, 2121, 4275, 999, 102]` against a quoted `[..., 19081, ...]`**, which is one token where the quote assumes `transformer` was whole.

d.title: Plain English costs all three exactly ten tokens; Hindi costs GPT-2 more than twice BERT
d.caption: **The differences only appear once you leave the distribution the vocabulary was built for.** Code costs BERT 27 against GPT-2's 24, and numbers 18 against 16 — **both cases where BERT's smaller, more English-word-oriented vocabulary has to split more.** Then the direction reverses: **Hindi costs BERT 11 tokens and GPT-2 26, and emoji 5 against 12**, because byte-level BPE spends one token per byte on text it has no merges for. **Which is a direct cost multiplier on every non-English prompt.**

d.title: Thirty thousand to a hundred and twenty-eight thousand, and the trend is upward
d.caption: The sizes track the era rather than the architecture: **BERT at 30,522 and LLaMA 2 at 32,000 against GPT-4 at ~100,000 and LLaMA 3 at 128,000.** The reason the number grew is §07's measurement — **a larger vocabulary buys shorter sequences on code and non-English text, which is where the token cost actually hurts** — and 4.10 §05 shows what makes it affordable: **a vocabulary is embedding parameters, and the embedding share falls as the model grows.**

d.title: Permutation-equivariance, proved and then measured at 1.91e-06
d.caption: **`P(·)Pᵀ` only relabels rows and columns and softmax is applied row-wise, so the permutation passes straight through: `Attn(PX) = P·Attn(X)`.** That is an identity about the mechanism, not a limitation of a particular model — **no amount of training changes it.** Verified on random matrices with permutation `[4, 1, 0, 5, 2, 3]`: **max absolute difference 1.91e-06, which is float noise.** So position has to be injected, and §02 is the catalogue of where.

d.title: Two axes, four quadrants, and one of them is nearly empty
d.caption: The axes are **absolute against relative** and **added to the input against applied inside attention** — and the quadrant map explains the field's history. **Absolute-at-the-input is where everything started: learned absolute and sinusoidal. Relative-inside-attention is where everything ended up: T5's bias, RoPE's rotation, ALiBi's linear penalty.** And **absolute-inside-attention is rare**, which is informative: once you are modifying attention directly, encoding distance is strictly more useful than encoding index.

d.title: Maximally flexible inside the trained length, and an index error outside it
d.caption: **GPT-2's context is 1024 and GPT-3's is 2048 for exactly this reason: the table has no row for index 2049, so the model does not degrade at longer lengths — it raises an index error.** Which is a different failure from every other scheme in this lesson, and arguably a better one: **a hard cap is visible.** The other cost is quieter: **`L_max × d` parameters spent on something a formula can compute for free**, which at GPT-2 small is 786,432 of them.

nodes.label: And costs L_max x d parameters
For what a formula computes free

d.title: The fast pair swings, the slow pair barely moves, and the rotation matrix does not depend on position
d.caption: At `d = 4` the two frequencies behave completely differently over the first three positions: **the fast pair goes 0.000 → 0.841 → 0.909 while the slow pair goes 0.000 → 0.010 → 0.020.** The derivation is the angle-addition identity per pair, and the consequence is the one that matters: **the rotation matrix depends on `k` but not on `pos`. So an absolute encoding already contains relative structure the model *can* learn to exploit — it just is not forced to. RoPE makes it the mechanism instead of a possibility.**

d.title: Shaw adds vectors to the keys; T5 adds one scalar to the logits
d.caption: The progression is a simplification. **Shaw adds a learned vector `a_{i−j}` to the keys inside attention, with distances clipped to ±k. T5 drops the vectors entirely: one learned *scalar* per (distance bucket, head), added straight to the attention logits, with no positional information in the input at all.** The bucketing is the clever part — **distances 0–7 get their own buckets, 8–11 share one, 12–15 another: fine resolution nearby and coarse far away**, which is cheap and a reasonable prior. **Total cost: a few thousand parameters for the whole model.**

d.title: Same relative distance, four absolute positions, the same score to five decimals
d.caption: **Rotate the query and key by an angle proportional to their absolute position, and because `R_mᵀR_n = R_{n−m}`, the dot product depends only on `n − m`.** Measured at `d = 64` with the same `q` and `k` at distance 3: **2.803810, 2.803811, 2.803815, 2.804198 at absolute positions 0, 10, 100 and 5000** — identical to five decimals, with the drift at 5000 being float precision. And it is not degenerate: **different distances give genuinely different scores**, from −0.727 at distance 0 to 1.761 at distance 2.

d.title: The decay is real when q and k are aligned and absent when they are random
d.caption: It is commonly stated that high-frequency pairs make distant contributions oscillate and cancel, giving a natural long-range decay. **Measured, the answer depends entirely on what you measure. With `q` and `k` identical — maximally aligned — the score falls to 0.0536 of its distance-0 value by 2048.** With 2,000 **independent random** pairs, **mean |score| is 6.42 at distance 0 and 6.39 at distance 2048 — no decay at all.** So **the decay is a property of aligned query-key pairs, not of the rotation**, which is a much weaker claim than the usual one.

steps.note: decay only in the left column

d.title: No positional embedding of any kind — just a penalty per head
d.caption: **Subtract `m_h·|i−j|` from the logits, with `m_h = 2^(-8h/H)`.** At `H = 8` the slopes come out as **exact powers of two: 1/2, 1/4, 1/8 … 1/256** — so **each head has a different effective window, from a head that sees almost nothing beyond a few tokens to one that is nearly position-blind.** That spread is the whole mechanism, and it is **fixed, not learned**, which is why ALiBi extrapolates best from train-short to test-long: there is nothing fitted to the training length.

d.title: Six schemes, and three of them cost zero parameters
d.caption: Read the parameter and extrapolation columns together. **Learned absolute spends `L_max × d` and extrapolates not at all. Sinusoidal, RoPE and ALiBi all cost zero** — and they differ in how far they stretch: **sinusoidal is defined beyond its training length and weak in practice, RoPE is good and becomes great with PI/NTK/YaRN scaling, and ALiBi is the best train-short-test-long of the set.** The deployed answer is the second-to-last row: **RoPE, in LLaMA, Mistral, Gemma and Qwen.**

d.title: Twelve blocks of 7,080,960, and the arithmetic reproduces exactly
d.caption: **The attention block is `4d²` — three projections plus the output — and the FFN is `2·d·d_ff`, which at `d_ff = 4d` is `8d²`. Twice the attention, as 4.6 established, and here it is in real numbers: 2,359,296 against 4,718,592.** Two LayerNorms add 3,072, which is 0.04% of the block. Then the embeddings: **38,597,376 for tokens and 786,432 for positions — the token embedding alone is nearly half of what the twelve blocks cost together.**

d.title: The two MLP matrices are 45% of the model, and the largest single tensor is not a layer
d.caption: The checkpoint is **124,439,808 against the arithmetic's 124,356,864 — a difference of 82,944, which is the biases the formula omitted.** Then the breakdown: **`c_fc` and `c_proj` together hold 56.6M, 45% of the entire model, against attention's 28.3M. And the single largest tensor is `wte.weight` at 38.6M, which is not a computation layer at all — it is a lookup table.** **Where the parameters are is not where most of the explanation goes.**

d.title: Four changes, and only one of them is free
d.caption: **Doubling layers doubles the parameters — cheap capacity, at the risk of training instability at depth. Doubling width quadruples them, and also widens every activation and the KV cache**, which is the part a parameter count hides. Doubling `d_ff` alone is 1.67× of the block, **targeted FFN capacity, common in MoE designs.** And **doubling heads at fixed `d_model` changes nothing at all** — it is the reshape from 4.4.

d.title: Thirty-one percent of GPT-2 small is embeddings, and two percent of LLaMA-2 7B
d.caption: **At small scale, vocabulary size is an architecture decision with real weight; at large scale it is close to free.** The share falls from **31.2% to 5.2% across the GPT-2 family and to 2.0% at LLaMA-2 7B** — so **a 30k-vocabulary model and a 128k one differ by a third of GPT-2 small and by a rounding error at 70B.** Which is exactly why the vocabularies in 4.8 §08 grew over time: **the token-efficiency win on code and non-English text stopped costing anything.** LLaMA-3's 7.5% is that decision, taken.

d.title: Four things the count does not tell you, and the last one is the important one
d.caption: **Training memory is roughly 4× the parameter memory before activations — weights, gradients and two Adam moments — so a 7B model in fp16 is about 14GB of weights and around 56GB before you store a single activation.** Compute has a usable rule: **forward is about `2 × params` FLOPs per token and training about `6 × params`.** And the honest last row: **parameter count correlates with capability only within an architecture family, and even then data and training compute matter more.**
